newsitem.title: ITALY: Priebke war crimes case switches track in Italy.
newsitem.headline: Priebke war crimes case switches track in Italy.

text.p: Italy's tortured efforts to stage an orderly war crimes trial for former SS captain Erich Priebke took another sharp turn on Thursday when military court authorities decided they were not competent to hear the case.

Judicial officials said a panel of military judges had met behind closed doors on Wednesday night and concluded that a civil court should decide whether Priebke was guilty of complicity in murder over Italy's worst World War Two atrocity.

Their ruling, reached without hearing legal argument from the prosecution or defence, brought Priebke's case into line with that of another SS veteran, former major Karl Hass, whose trial is being sought in Italy for the same atrocity.

But it also raised the question of why the 83-year-old German, held in detention since his extradition from Argentina 13 months ago, had been tried by a military court in the first place for the 1944 massacre of 335 men and boys.
That trial, dogged by legal challenges, ended in uproar in August when the court found Priebke guilty but ruled he was no longer liable for punishment. The verdict has since been declared void.
Military magistrate Antonino Intelisano, who led the prosecution at Priebke's first trial, said he had learned of the latest twist in the case only on Thursday morning.
"I am very bitter at what has happened but I can do nothing about it," Intelisano told Reuters.

He said civil judges would now have to decide whether they were competent to try Priebke but that a ruling may have to go to Italy's highest court, the Court of Cassation, spelling further delay in the case.

Priebke and Hass are both accused of complicity in multiple murder for their acknowledged participation in the Ardeatine Caves massacre south of Rome in March 1944, when 335 men and boys were shot in reprisal for a partisan bomb attack.
Both men argue that they were under orders to take part in the massacre and would have been killed had they refused.

Hass, who had testified at Priebke's first trial after breaking his pelvis in a bizarre attempt to flee by clambering over the balcony of a guarded hotel room in Rome, was brought before a military judge for a committal hearing last month.

The judge, Giuseppe Mazzi, ruled that the SS was not an orthodox military organisation and that the matter should therefore be dealt with by a civil court. Hass, 84, was released from house arrest pending further developments.
Relatives of victims of the Caves massacre, who were civil plaintiffs at Priebke's first trial, had argued throughout that a military court was the wrong forum to judge the case.
They welcomed the latest ruling, while expressing regret that a proper verdict had so far eluded all concerned.
"If it wasn't so tragic it would be comic, and we are all the more bitter because of that," said Rosina Stame, who was six when her father was shot at the Ardeatine Caves.

"We don't want a vendetta, we want justice and clarity. There has got to be a verdict that is not an insult to the victims and their relatives and a trial that doesn't make Italy a laughing stock," she said.
German authorities have asked for the extradition of Priebke and Hass but Italian proceedings take precedence.
